name: Blow-dry and volumizing routine

card.summary: Drying hair upward with a dryer for temporary root lift; no trials, and the effect washes out.
card.note: Repeated high heat is described as drying hair.

quick.overview:
A blow-dry and volumizing routine means drying hair with a dryer while lifting it at the roots so the style sets with more height. It is a styling technique rather than a treatment.

No published studies were found that test it for volume. The effect is temporary.
quick.mechanism: Dryers are described as setting hair by forming temporary hydrogen bonds in each strand, which humidity and washing reverse. Nozzles and diffusers change how air and heat reach the hair.
quick.risks: Hair-care references note that heat from dryers can leave hair dry and brittle with heavy use. Tool-related skin reactions, such as nickel contact allergy from a brush, have been reported in case literature.

lead: A blow-dry and volumizing routine is a hair-styling practice in which hair is dried with a handheld dryer, often while being lifted or directed upward at the roots, to give a hairstyle more height and body. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and grooming circles as a low-cost way to change the apparent fullness of the hair, which in turn changes the shape of the head and the frame around the face.

Hair dryers shape hair by speeding up and controlling the formation of temporary hydrogen bonds in each strand; these bonds disappear after washing, and brushes, combs and styling products used during drying can add hold and lift.[1] A cool-air setting is described as helping set a style and reduce frizz, and diffusers are described as giving a slower, cooler dry that reduces frizz and adds volume for fine or curly hair.[1] Blow-drying is also described as a temporary method, with results tending to revert on exposure to water or humidity.[4]

No published clinical studies have tested blow-drying routines for volume. General hair-care references note that heat from dryers and hot irons can leave hair dry and brittle when overused, and that heat protectant sprays can reduce damage.[2][4]

angle.text: Blow-drying with root lift gives hair visible body and height for the day, which practitioners use to make thinning or flat hair look fuller and to frame the face. The effect is temporary and resets with washing.

paras: In a volumizing blow-dry, hair is typically dried while sections are lifted away from the scalp or directed upward, so that the hair sets in a raised position. A cool-air burst at the end is described in dryer references as helping to hold the shape and reduce frizz.[1]

Attachments change how the airflow reaches the hair. A concentrator narrows the airflow to focus heat and speed up drying, while a comb nozzle combines a concentrator with comb-like teeth.[1] A diffuser spreads the airflow, drying hair more slowly and at a lower temperature, which is described as adding volume and reducing frizz for fine, coloured, permed or curly hair.[1] Ionic dryers aim to reduce static, though Wikipedia notes their effectiveness is debated.[1]

Wikipedia's article on blowouts describes pairing a dryer with a round brush or comb attachment, using low to medium heat, and using leave-in conditioner or large rollers on damp hair as ways to limit heat exposure.[4] It also describes the Dominican blowout, which was popularised in the United States by Dominican stylists and became popular among African American women as a chemical-free way to straighten hair.[4]

Alexandre Godefroy built a large seated salon dryer in 1888, and Gabriel Kazanjian patented a hair dryer in the US in 1911.[1] Handheld models appeared around 1920, although early ones were heavy and low-wattage, and plastic bodies in the 1950s and 1960s made dryers lighter.[1] In 1991 the US Consumer Product Safety Commission required ground fault circuit interrupters in dryers.[1]

General hair-care references state that hair overheated by dryers and hot irons can become dry and brittle and that heat is among the traumas that can lead to split ends.[2] A 1982 dermatology report described contact allergy to nickel from a blow-dry hair brush, an example of tool-related skin reactions.[3]
